hints: Count the total carbon and hydrogen atoms in $(CH_3)_2CHCH_3$ and in $CH_3(CH_2)_2CH_3$ and compare their molecular formulae.
Look at how the carbons are joined together, one is a straight chain and the other is branched, and recall what must differ for isomers.
walkthrough:
Check what is the same**
Think of molecular formula as the atom count. Expand both in your head. Butane $CH_3(CH_2)_2CH_3$ is $4$ carbons and $10$ hydrogens. Methylpropane $(CH_3)_2CHCH_3$ is also $4$ carbons and $10$ hydrogens. So both are $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$. That sameness is the first half of being isomers.

Check what is different**
Now picture the skeleton. Butane is a straight chain of four carbons in a row. Methylpropane has three carbons in a row with a branch on the middle carbon. The atoms are joined in a different order, so the structural formulae are different. Same formula plus different structure means isomers.

Final answer: Both compounds have the same molecular formula, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$.
They have different structural formulae (different arrangement of atoms).

hints: Recall that when only the carbon skeleton arrangement differs, with no functional group or position change, a specific type of structural isomerism is involved.
walkthrough:
Link branching to the name**
Both molecules are alkanes, so there is no functional group to move and no double bond for stereoisomerism. The only difference is the carbon chain, straight versus branched. In AS chemistry you can call this structural isomerism, and more precisely chain isomerism.

hints: Use the sign of $\Delta H = -8.0 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for the forward reaction to decide whether heat is released or absorbed going from butane to methylpropane.
Think about how the system opposes an increase in temperature by favouring the reaction direction that takes in heat.
walkthrough:
Read the energy clue**
The equation shows $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CH}_3(\text{g}) \rightleftharpoons (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_3(\text{g})$ with $\Delta H = -8.0 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. A negative sign means the forward change from butane to methylpropane gives out heat. It is exothermic, so the reverse change is endothermic.

Apply the oppose the change idea**
If you heat the mixture to $473 \text{ K}$, the system tries to cool itself down by taking in extra heat. That means it favours the endothermic direction, which here is backwards, from methylpropane back to butane. So at the new equilibrium there is less methylpropane and more butane.

Final answer: The forward reaction is exothermic ($\Delta H$ is negative).
Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium to the left (in the endothermic direction), so the proportion of methylpropane decreases and the proportion of butane increases.

hints: Recall what the amounts do with time once forward and reverse rates become equal in a closed system.
walkthrough:
Spot when change stops**
At the start the falling curve is butane being used up and the rising curve is methylpropane being formed. While the lines are sloping, amounts are still changing. When both lines go flat and horizontal, amounts stay constant. That flat start is dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse reactions still happening but with no net change. Mark $t$ exactly where the flat part begins.
Final answer: $t$ marked at the time where both curves first become horizontal (flat, constant amount), about where amount of butane $= 0.3$ mol and amount of methylpropane $= 0.7$ mol.

hints: Read the flat plateau values for each curve in mol, then use the $1 \text{ dm}^3$ vessel volume to convert to $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.
walkthrough:
Read then convert**
Look at the right hand flat region. The lower curve, which started at $1.0$ mol, levels at $0.3$ mol. That is butane. The upper curve, which started at $0$, levels at $0.7$ mol. That is methylpropane. Because concentration $= \text{moles} / \text{volume}$ and volume $= 1 \text{ dm}^3$, the numbers stay the same but units become $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. So $0.3 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ butane and $0.7 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ methylpropane.

Final answer: concentration of butane $= 0.3 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$
concentration of methylpropane $= 0.7 \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$

hints: Remember the general rule for $K_c$, products on top divided by reactants, with each concentration raised to its balancing number.
walkthrough:
Build products over reactants**
For $K_c$ you always put equilibrium concentration of products on the top and reactants on the bottom. Here the reaction is $1:1$ with no big numbers, so no powers are needed:
$$K_{\text{c}} = \frac{\text{[(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{3}\text{]}}{\text{[CH}_{3}\text{(CH}_{2}\text{)}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}\text{]}}$$

hints: Substitute the two equilibrium concentrations from (c)(ii) into the $K_c$ expression from (c)(iii), product divided by reactant.
Think about whether any concentration units cancel in this $1:1$ isomerisation, $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ divided by $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$.
walkthrough:
Substitute and divide**
Put your equilibrium values straight in:
$$K_{\text{c}} = \frac{0.7}{0.3} = 2.33$$
Keep two or three significant figures, $2.33$ is ideal. The total moles check out too, $0.3 + 0.7 = 1.0$ mol, so no gas has escaped.

Sort the units**
Both top and bottom have units $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$. When you divide them they cancel completely:
$$\frac{\text{mol dm}^{-3}}{\text{mol dm}^{-3}} = 1$$
So $K_c$ for this isomerisation has no units. It is dimensionless.

Final answer: $K_{\text{c}} = 0.7 / 0.3 = 2.33$
units = none (no units / dimensionless)
